# Autonomous Agents {#sec-front-autonomous}

An autonomous agent runs without a human in each loop: it sets its own
subgoals, runs for long horizons, and commits real actions. This chapter
explains the design questions that are still open: how to keep a long
running agent on task, how to bound what it can do, and how to know whether
it is working. By the end a reader can frame the autonomy problem and the
trade-offs each proposed answer makes.

## Problem

Removing the human raises the stakes of every failure mode from the
agentic loop. The agent must stay aligned with intent over a long horizon,
recover from its own mistakes, and not take an irreversible wrong action,
with no turn-by-turn supervisor.

## Design

Long-horizon planning with durable memory and goal state, guardrails and
permission boundaries around actions, and human oversight moved from
in-the-loop to on-the-loop. The open question is how much structure to
impose versus how much to learn.

## Evolution

From supervised agentic loops, to early autonomous task runners, to
sandboxed long-running agents with explicit oversight and permission
models. Trace which failures each generation was built to contain.

## Trade-offs

Autonomy buys scale and unattended work at the cost of predictability and
safety. Tighter guardrails buy safety at the cost of capability. Durable
memory buys coherence and accumulates error and drift.

## In practice

Permission and sandbox models, checkpointing a long-running agent,
oversight interfaces, kill switches, and evaluating behavior over long
horizons where a single trajectory is not enough.

## Foundations

The theory under the open questions. Autonomy as control over a long
horizon, the alignment problem stated precisely, corrigibility, and the
limits of oversight when actions outpace review.
